## Purpose and scope

This guide is the standalone reference for the UIAO Git substrate's
active-passive replication posture. It consolidates the replication content
previously embedded in the Platform Server Build Guide and the Disaster
Recovery Playbook into a single operational surface, and adds the
monitoring, failover-test, and encryption-verification requirements needed
to operate replication as a governed control rather than a one-time setup.

The architectural decision that establishes this topology is recorded in
ADR-041 (Git infrastructure on Windows Server 2025 + IIS) and extended by
ADR-090 (substrate high availability — hot-standby replica with
split-brain-safe failover). This guide is the operator-facing companion to
those decisions; it does not change them.

### Topology

The substrate runs one **active (primary)** Git host that serves all read
and write traffic, and one **passive (standby)** host that continuously
receives replicated state. A third copy — the GitHub mirror — provides an
off-site, read-only durability tier. The standby is promoted to active only
during a declared failover.

| Role | Serves traffic | State source | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| Active (primary) | Yes (read + write) | Authoritative | Normal operations |
| Passive (standby) | No (until promoted) | Replicated from primary | Local recovery / fast failover |
| GitHub mirror | Read-only | Pushed from primary | Off-site durability |

## Replication mechanism

Repository state replicates from the active host to the passive host on
every accepted push. The `post-receive` governance hook on the primary
triggers the replication push to the standby's bare repositories, so the
standby is brought current as part of the same operation that records the
push — there is no separate, lossy batch job in the normal path. A periodic
reconciliation sweep re-pushes any refs that a transient failure left behind
and confirms the standby's ref set matches the primary.

## Replication monitoring (`SI-4`, `AU-6`)

Replication is monitored, not assumed. The following signals are collected
and alerted on:

- **Replication lag** — the time and ref delta between the primary's tip and
  the standby's tip for each repository. Lag beyond a defined threshold
  (default: any ref more than 5 minutes behind) raises an alert.
- **Replication failures** — a failed replication push (network, auth, or
  disk) is logged on the primary and surfaces immediately; repeated failures
  escalate to an incident under the Incident Response Plan.
- **Standby liveness** — the standby is health-checked on a fixed interval;
  loss of liveness is treated as a degraded-redundancy condition even while
  the primary still serves traffic.
- **Mirror freshness** — the GitHub mirror's last successful push timestamp
  is tracked so the off-site tier cannot silently fall stale.

Replication-lag and failure events are correlated with the drift engine: an
unexplained divergence between primary and standby ref sets is treated as a
`DRIFT-PROVENANCE` integrity signal, not merely an availability event.

## Failover and failback

A failover is a **declared** action, never automatic for write traffic
without the split-brain protections defined in ADR-090. The high-level
sequence is:

1. Declare the primary unavailable per the Disaster Recovery Playbook
   decision tree and confirm it is fenced (cannot accept writes).
2. Verify the standby's ref set is current (or accept and record the known
   data delta if the primary failed mid-replication).
3. Promote the standby to active and repoint the IIS reverse proxy / DNS.
4. Resume operations; the GitHub mirror continues as the off-site tier.

Failback to the original primary reverses the flow only after the original
host is rebuilt to baseline, re-synchronized from the current active, and
verified — it is never assumed healthy on the basis of having been primary
before.

### Failover test schedule (`CP-4`)

Failover is exercised on a schedule, not only during real incidents:

- **Quarterly** — a non-disruptive verification that the standby is current
  and promotable (ref-set comparison plus a promotion dry-run in an isolated
  context).
- **Annually** — a full functional failover test that promotes the standby,
  serves traffic from it, and fails back, performed within a maintenance
  window. Results, the measured recovery time against the RTO, and any gaps
  are recorded, and corrective actions are tracked as POA&M items.

## Encryption verification (`SC-8`, `SC-28`)

Replicated data is protected both in transit and at rest, and that
protection is verified rather than presumed:

- **In transit (`SC-8`)** — replication pushes between primary and standby,
  and to the GitHub mirror, traverse TLS. Verification confirms the
  transport negotiates an approved TLS version and cipher suite (enforced by
  the host Schannel baseline) and that TLS verification is not disabled on
  the replication path.
- **At rest (`SC-28`)** — the primary, standby, and any backup volumes are
  encrypted at rest (BitLocker on the Windows hosts). Verification confirms
  encryption is enabled and the protectors are healthy on every node that
  holds a copy of the repository state, including the standby.

Encryption verification is part of the quarterly failover verification above,
so a node that has silently lost its at-rest protection cannot remain a
sanctioned copy of the substrate.

## Summary of controls

| Area | Control(s) | Requirement |
|---|---|---|
| Replication monitoring | `SI-4`, `AU-6` | Lag, failure, liveness, and mirror-freshness signals are collected and alerted |
| Failover testing | `CP-4` | Quarterly verification, annual functional failover test, results recorded |
| Encryption in transit | `SC-8` | Replication paths use approved TLS; verification not disabled |
| Encryption at rest | `SC-28` | All copies (primary, standby, backups) encrypted; protectors verified |
| Integrity | `SI-7` | Primary/standby divergence treated as a provenance/integrity signal |
